tagline.text: A slow half day in the forest that guards Manila's water

location.label: Location
location.text: Greater Lagro, Quezon City, Metro Manila (below La Mesa Dam)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱150–1,500 per person (transport from central Manila, admission and activities)

children.text: A
33-hectare

forest park on the edge of the protected watershed below La Mesa Reservoir, Metro Manila's water source. It suits a relaxed half-day outing of slow walks around the lagoon, ponds, Butterfly Garden and forest trails, with a packed lunch in the shade.
La Mesa Ecopark is a forest park just below La Mesa Dam, between Fairview and Novaliches at the northern tip of Quezon City. The park covers about
33 hectares
, and behind it stretches the La Mesa Watershed Reservation, about
2,659 hectares
in size. Hardly any forest of this size survives inside Metro Manila, with its high-rises and gridlocked roads, so locals have long called it the city's lungs.
La Mesa Dam, above the park, was built in
during the American colonial era as the Novaliches Reservoir and stands about

high. It is the last reservoir in the Angat–Ipo–La Mesa system, collecting water that flows down from Angat and Ipo dams, and most of Metro Manila's water supply passes through this system. The forest in the park is therefore a buffer that keeps soil and pollution out of the reservoir before it is a playground, and most of the reservation is closed to the public.
Today's park is the result of work that began in

, when Bantay Kalikasan, the environmental arm of the ABS-CBN Foundation, led by environmentalist Gina Lopez, replanted the bare watershed and restored an old resort area. After about 25 years the foundation returned management to the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), and the park closed in
February 2024
. On
the Manila Water Foundation took over together with MWSS and the Quezon City government and reopened it starting with Phase 1. Phase 2, with the lagoon and ponds, reopened on
August 1, 2026
, and all three phases are now in operation.

The swimming pool, zipline, pedal boats and horseback riding mentioned in older guides are not on the official list since the reopening, so visitors expecting those rides may be disappointed. Instead the focus is on quiet nature experiences such as shaded forest walks, the Butterfly Garden, birdwatching, fishing, cycling and team-building activities. It suits families with children, residents looking for a weekend morning workout, and travelers staying in Manila who are craving a day of greenery.

blocks.title: Lagoon walk past rows of nipa huts

children.text: The Phase 2 lagoon is the park's signature view. Nipa huts with palm-leaf roofs line the shore, and the forest is mirrored on the calm water. Walking around the lagoon is included in admission, and the huts can be rented separately for a picnic.

Near the lagoon are Neptune Pond and a koi pond where colorful carp swim. Shaded rest spots surround the water lilies, making it a pleasant place to sit for a while. Viewing the ponds is also included in admission.

Climb the steps up a flower-planted hill and a viewing deck looks down over the lagoon and forest. There are quite a few steps, so comfortable shoes help. Flower Hill charges a small fee on top of admission.
Netted enclosures and flower beds let you see many kinds of butterflies up close, which children especially love. The separate fee is reported to be about
, and the best time to visit is a sunny morning when butterflies are most active.
The Nature Trail is the densest forest path, bordering the protected reservation. The separate fee is about
, and walking early in the morning gives you a good chance of spotting birds such as kingfishers and sunbirds. The trail is dirt and gets slippery after rain, so wear sneakers.

Phase 1 has the BiodiverCity exhibit introducing the plants and animals of the La Mesa watershed, a small museum and an eco viewing deck. Learning first why this forest protects Manila's water makes the park look different as you walk.

The park roads and short forest paths are good for cycling, and rental bikes are available. In the woods there is a bamboo team-building course and a climbing wall, popular with school and company groups. Group activities are best booked in advance.

items.title: Half-day course by public transport
items.subtitle: A morning trip by MRT and bus

children.text: Take MRT-3 from North Avenue Station to Quezon Avenue Station, then catch a bus toward Commonwealth Avenue at the EDSA intersection.
Get off at the Commonwealth Avenue–Pearl Drive intersection and walk about
or take a tricycle to the ticket booth on Dunhill Street.
Enter as soon as the park opens and start with the museum and BiodiverCity exhibit in Phase 1.
Walk the Nature Trail in the cool morning listening to birdsong, then stop by the Butterfly Garden.
Head down to Phase 2 and see the lagoon, Neptune Pond and the Flower Hill viewing deck in turn.
Rest with the snacks you brought in the shade by the lagoon or in a picnic area.
Leave the park before it gets hot, have lunch at a mall in Fairview and head back.
Commonwealth Avenue is badly congested at rush hour, so the earlier you set off the easier the trip. On the way back, leaving late in the afternoon also risks the evening rush.

items.title: Family picnic course
items.subtitle: Come by car and relax in the shade

children.text: Pack lunch boxes, a picnic mat and water, and set off by car or Grab.
Buy tickets on arrival, and if you plan to use a nipa hut or pavilion, rent it at the ticket booth first.
See the Butterfly Garden and the koi pond with the children.
Try fishing in the fishing area or rent bikes for a loop of the park roads.
Have lunch and rest in a lagoon-side hut or a picnic area.
Look around the amphitheater lawn and Flower Hill, then leave the park at an easy pace.
The park closes at
, so start packing up by around
at the latest. Huts and pavilions fill up quickly on weekends and holidays, so arrive early.
From abroad or other provinces, fly into Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL). The park is about
30km
by road from the airport,
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
by car depending on traffic. Rather than going on your arrival day, spend a night in central Manila and go the next morning.
Take MRT-3 and get off at Quezon Avenue Station. It is one stop from North Avenue Station, and the fare is about
At the Quezon Avenue–EDSA intersection, take Bus Route 6 (Sapang Palay–PITX), which runs along Commonwealth Avenue, and get off at the Pearl Drive intersection. The fare is about
Other buses or UV Express vans heading to SM Fairview along Commonwealth Avenue also stop at Pearl Drive. Tell the conductor in advance that you are getting off at Pearl Drive.
MRT-7 is under construction along Commonwealth Avenue but has not yet opened as of
Grab is the easiest option. From Makati or BGC it is about
25km
by road,
1–2 hours
by car, and costs about
one way. Entering La Mesa Ecopark as the destination takes you to the Dunhill Street entrance. Cars can be hard to find outside the park on the way back, so book through the app ahead of time.

Drive along Commonwealth Avenue toward Fairview, turn right onto Pearl Drive and then into Dunhill Street. Roads around the park get busy on weekend mornings, so arrive early. Follow on-site guidance on whether parking is available and how much it costs.
From the Pearl Drive intersection to the ticket booth takes about
10–15 minutes
on foot. If you have bags or it is hot, take a tricycle from the intersection for about
. Inside the park you get around on foot; the sections are not far apart, but there are slopes and stairs.
Metro Manila's dry season runs
December–May
and the rainy season
June–November
. The best time for walking is
December–February
, when the northeast monsoon blows and morning temperatures of around
make the forest trails refreshing.
March–May
is almost rainless, but midday temperatures climb above
, so explore in the morning right after opening.
In the rainy season there are afternoon showers almost daily, and typhoons pass through in
July–October

. Rain makes the dirt paths slippery and some sections may close after heavy rain, so check the official Facebook page for notices. The forest is greenest after rain, and the morning after a downpour is actually great for photos. Weekends, holidays and school breaks bring many families, while weekday mornings are the quietest.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of 2026 and may vary depending on local conditions.

There is no accommodation for ordinary travelers inside the park, so most people visit as a day trip. If you are staying in central Manila, Makati or BGC, simply set off early in the morning; to stay closer, hotels around Quezon Avenue and North Avenue in Quezon City are convenient. Mid-range hotels in this area cost about
per night.

Food inside the park is limited to snack-stand fare. Filipino families usually bring rice, adobo, grilled meat and pancit from home and share them in the picnic areas or huts. Doing the same with lunch boxes and water from a convenience store or mall makes things easy. Head north along Commonwealth Avenue from the park and you reach SM City Fairview, with everything from fast food to Filipino restaurants.
Opening hours are Tuesday to Sunday,
, and the park closes on Mondays for maintenance. When a Monday is a public holiday, check the official Facebook page to see whether it opens.

At the 2024 reopening only visitors with online reservations could enter, and many recent visitor reviews say walk-ins are now accepted. Entry rules may change, so check the official Facebook page before you go.
Quezon City residents with a QCitizen ID enter free and are asked to follow the park's Facebook page or Instagram account. If you live in Quezon City, bring your ID.
For birds and butterflies,
7–9 AM
, right after opening, is best. Binoculars make it much easier to see birds along the forest edge.
Bring cash for admission and activity fees. Plenty of small bills makes it easier when moving between ticket counters.
Bring mosquito repellent, water and a hat. There is plenty of forest shade, but the humidity makes you sweat more than you expect.
Schools or companies planning team-building activities or wanting to use a pavilion or the amphitheater should contact the park in advance for the schedule and rates.
Check the park map on the board near the ticket booth, and since open facilities can differ by section, ask staff what is open that day to avoid wasted trips.

La Mesa Reservoir and the watershed reservation behind the park are Metro Manila's drinking water source and cannot be entered without permission. Do not leave the marked paths and open areas, and do not climb the fences on the reservoir side.
The swimming pool, zipline, pedal boats and horseback riding mentioned in older posts are not on the current official list. Do not pack a swimsuit based only on old blogs or videos.
Dirt paths and stairs are slippery after rain. Hold children's hands and walk slowly on the Flower Hill steps and the Nature Trail.
The forest is a wildlife habitat. Do not feed birds or animals or pick plants, and take all your trash home.
Admission, activity fees and open sections have changed often during redevelopment. Check the latest notices before your visit.
Commonwealth Avenue around the park carries heavy, fast traffic. After getting off the bus, use footbridges or traffic lights to cross.
